item.title: Radda centre resumes services for 250 mothers, children daily
item.description:
Doctors are working to restore and expand healthcare services at the Radda MCH-FP Centre, a private mother and child health facility in Mirpur-1, Dhaka, despite the centre having been demolished. Renovation work is also under way at its vaccination unit.
During a visit to the centre on Thursday, this correspondent found that the damaged boundary walls had been rebuilt and painted, with a new gate installed. One of the damaged rooms had also been cleaned and renovated.
The renovated entrance of the Radda MCH-FP Centre in Mirpur-1, Dhaka, following its demolition. Photo: Dhaka Tribune
Health workers had arranged tables and chairs in one room, while eight to 10 chairs were placed on the two verandas for mothers and children waiting for vaccination.
However, the absence of fans left patients struggling in the heat, with several children seen crying.
Debris, including broken concrete and bricks, had been cleared from several rooms. Doctors and health workers were providing services in two rooms, while renovation work continued in others.
A vaccination banner was visible at the entrance, where children were weighed and their vaccination cards filled out before being taken inside for services.
Dr Ripa Das, a physician at the centre, told Dhaka Tribune that vaccination services were fully operational, although all facilities had not yet been restored.
“Ultrasonogram services have not resumed, and we do not have a laboratory yet,” she said.
She added that the centre, which has been serving patients for around 50 years, receives a large number of patients.
“We hope to resume ultrasound services in November. We are also trying to complete the remaining renovation work as quickly as possible,” she said.
Radda Executive Director Dr Nasrin Akhter told Dhaka Tribune: “We are very grateful to the media for standing by us during that difficult time.”
She also thanked State Minister for Youth and Sports Md Aminul Haque for providing financial assistance.
Renovation work is continuing, she said, expressing hope that the centre would soon be able to restore healthcare services for mothers and children on the scale required.
Child vaccination began at around 10:30am in one of the centre's damaged rooms. After the demolition, vaccination services had been provided under a roadside tarpaulin outside the facility. They have now moved back inside.
Samanta Begum, a resident of Mirpur, brought her eight-month-old daughter, Ayat, for vaccination.
“I have been bringing Ayat here for vaccination since birth. Her father was also vaccinated here. I was very worried when I heard that the hospital had been demolished. I wondered where I would get my baby vaccinated. We are relieved that the hospital has not closed. The services here are very good,” she told Dhaka Tribune.
Nijhum Akhter brought her six-month-old son, Sadat, for a measles vaccine.
“Child vaccination and family planning services are available, but the ultrasonogram and laboratory facilities destroyed during the demolition have not yet been restored,” she said.
She added that the centre previously offered ultrasound services at a nominal cost, making them accessible to low-income families.
“I hope the government will look into the matter and take steps to restore these services,” she said.
Dr Tania Nowrin Jui, a physician at the National Institute of Ophthalmology and Hospital, also visited the centre to have her child vaccinated.
“The services here are very good. We live in Mirpur, and both my baby and I received vaccinations here when I was a child,” she told Dhaka Tribune.
Nur-Mohammad, who is in charge of the centre's vaccination unit, told Dhaka Tribune that around 250 mothers and children receive services there every day, compared with approximately 350 before the demolition.
Alongside Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI) services, the centre is also providing measles vaccinations.
“Once the renovation work is complete, we will be able to serve more patients. For now, we are collecting samples and sending them to other laboratories for testing,” he said.

item.title: Bangladesh’s renewable energy ambition faces a race against time
item.description:
Bangladesh's ambition to significantly expand renewable energy by 2030 faces major challenges, with current installed capacity still below 2,000 megawatts (MW) and billions of dollars in investment needed to meet its targets.
Land shortages, regulatory hurdles and limitations in the electricity grid continue to slow the transition, highlighting the gap between the country's renewable energy ambitions and its current capacity.
The challenge is becoming increasingly urgent. The country must move beyond policy announcements and project tenders to deliver operational power plants, encourage households and industries to adopt rooftop solar, attract private investment and modernize its electricity network.
The government has set a target of generating 10,000MW of renewable electricity by 2030, while the Renewable Energy Policy 2025 aims to meet at least 20% of national electricity demand from renewable sources by 2030 and 30% by 2040.
A revised target of installing 10,450MW by 2030 has raised the stakes further. According to energy analysts, meeting that target will require a significant acceleration in implementation, with thousands of megawatts added every year.
The central question is no longer whether Bangladesh needs a clean-energy transition, but whether its institutions, investors and electricity infrastructure can deliver it at the required pace.
Bangladesh's installed renewable energy capacity stood at 1,935.79MW, according to Shahriar Ahmed Chowdhury, director of the Centre for Energy Research at United International University.
Solar accounts for 1,642.7MW of that capacity, followed by hydropower at 230MW and wind power at 62MW. The figures demonstrate the country's heavy reliance on solar and the relatively limited contribution of other renewable sources.
Chowdhury estimated that Bangladesh would need at least 12,000MW of renewable energy capacity by 2030 and more than 35,000MW by 2040.
The Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) has estimated that annual additions of around 760MW would take Bangladesh's renewable capacity to nearly 5,850MW by 2030.
The Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), however, has presented a substantially higher projection. Based on estimated electricity demand of 22,702MW in 2030, it calculated that a 20% renewable share would require 4,540MW of renewable electricity generation.
Accounting for the operating characteristics of renewable power plants, CPD estimated that installed capacity would need to reach approximately 18,162MW to produce that amount of electricity. For 2040, it projected a renewable capacity requirement of 35,713MW.
These estimates are not directly interchangeable. Installed capacity represents the maximum rated output of power plants, whereas generation measures the electricity actually produced over time. Solar and wind output varies according to sunlight, weather and operating conditions.
Nevertheless, the differences highlight a major planning challenge. Bangladesh needs a clearly defined national roadmap explaining how its renewable energy targets translate into installed capacity, actual generation and annual project requirements.
Using the reported installed capacity of 1,935.79MW, the country would need an additional 4,209MW to reach the 6,145MW estimate, more than 10,000MW to meet Chowdhury's 12,000MW projection and approximately 16,226MW to reach CPD's 18,162MW estimate.
These comparisons are based on different projections, not separate official government targets. However, they illustrate the scale of the challenge and the need for clarity about what the government intends to achieve by 2030.
Bangladesh has initiated tenders for 55 ground-mounted solar projects with a combined proposed capacity of 5,238MW, according to information cited in the source material.
A ministry official indicated that implementation could extend until 2028. If the projects secure financing, obtain land and regulatory approvals, complete construction and connect to the national grid on schedule, they could make a substantial contribution to renewable generation.
However, proposed capacity is not the same as operational capacity. A tender announcement does not guarantee financing, construction or timely commissioning. Delays at any stage could reduce the contribution these projects make before the 2030 deadline.
The government needs to establish how many projects have secured financing, how much land is ready, which projects have entered construction and when they are expected to begin commercial operations.
Without publicly available project-level information, it remains difficult to determine how much of the proposed 5,238MW could realistically reach the grid within the available timeframe.
Rooftop solar offers another route to expanding renewable generation, particularly in a densely populated country where acquiring large areas of land for ground-mounted installations can be difficult.
In June 2025, then chief adviser Muhammad Yunus directed the authorities to pursue a National Rooftop Solar Program, including installations on government buildings. The initiative also envisaged private companies installing rooftop systems to help schools, colleges and madrasas reduce their electricity bills.
The previous interim government had set a target of installing 3,000MW of rooftop solar capacity by December 2025. However, an earlier analysis reported that only 245MW had been installed between 2008 and mid-2025.
More recent figures attributed to the Sustainable and Renewable Energy Development Authority (SREDA) put rooftop solar capacity at 565.55MW, including net-metered and non-net-metered installations.
The reported breakdown includes 468.38MWp from net-metered rooftop solar systems, with more than 5,190 systems integrated into the national grid, and 93.71MWp from non-net-metered systems, comprising around 468 non-grid-tied or traditional auxiliary installations.
Although the figures indicate progress, rooftop capacity remains considerably below the earlier 3,000MW target. Regularly updated official statistics are needed to establish how quickly the program is expanding and whether household and institutional participation is accelerating.
Industry could become an important driver of this expansion. For businesses facing electricity costs, rooftop solar can reduce dependence on grid power while improving energy-cost predictability.
However, household adoption will depend on the attractiveness of incentives, access to financing, installation costs and practical arrangements for connecting rooftop systems to the grid.
Floating solar installations on suitable water bodies could provide another option where land is scarce. Their development, however, requires careful assessment of potential impacts on fisheries, aquatic ecosystems, navigation and the livelihoods of communities dependent on those water bodies.
Even if Bangladesh identifies enough viable projects, financing could become one of the most significant barriers to the transition.
Imran Karim, former president of the Bangladesh Independent Power Producers' Association, estimated that achieving the 20% renewable energy target by 2030 would require investment of $12 billion to $14 billion.
CPD estimated that achieving a 30% renewable energy share by 2040 could require $35.2 billion to $42.6 billion. The estimates relate to different targets and timeframes and should not be treated as directly comparable.
The Renewable Energy Policy 2025 offers corporate tax exemptions to renewable energy producers for the first 10 years, followed by partial exemptions for another 5 years. The government has also announced the removal of duties on solar technologies and equipment.
However, fiscal incentives alone may not be sufficient to attract the required investment. Developers continue to face financing costs, foreign-exchange exposure, land availability, regulatory uncertainty and the commercial terms governing electricity purchases.
Chowdhury identified lengthy approval procedures, the need to secure around 40 permits, a 6-year lock-in period for lead partners, grid constraints and Bangladesh's BB- investment risk rating among the barriers to investment.
Land requirements add another layer of complexity. Chowdhury estimated that ground-mounted solar projects could require around 3 acres per MW, although actual requirements vary according to technology and site conditions. At that rate, a 1,000MW project could require approximately 3,000 acres.
For a densely populated country where agricultural land, settlements and infrastructure compete for space, large-scale solar development requires careful site selection and planning.
A streamlined approval process, transparent procurement, bankable power-purchase arrangements and clearer responsibilities among government agencies could reduce uncertainty and help developers move projects from planning to construction.
Building renewable power plants is only one part of the transition. Bangladesh must also ensure that its electricity system can absorb, transmit and deliver the power they generate.
Solar output fluctuates with sunlight and weather, while wind generation depends on changing wind conditions. As the share of variable renewable energy rises, the power system will need stronger transmission networks, battery storage and flexible generation reserves to maintain reliable electricity supplies.
Without adequate infrastructure, newly built renewable plants could face difficulties connecting to the grid or delivering electricity when required.
Chowdhury has emphasized the importance of battery storage and flexible reserves. He has also warned that inconsistencies between energy policy documents could expose investments to the risk of becoming stranded assets.
The government's grid-modernization program will therefore be critical. Transmission planning must progress alongside renewable project development rather than becoming a bottleneck after power plants are completed.
Regional comparisons indicate considerable room for Bangladesh to expand solar power. Figures attributed to a 2024 International Renewable Energy Agency report and cited at a Waterkeepers Bangladesh event put solar's share of electricity demand at 24% in India, 17.16% in Pakistan, 39.7% in Sri Lanka and 5.6% in Bangladesh.
The figures suggest a substantial gap, although a definitive comparison requires confirmation that the countries use consistent definitions, reporting periods and measurement methods.
Ultimately, Bangladesh's energy transition will be judged not by the number of policies, targets or tenders announced, but by how much affordable and reliable renewable electricity reaches the national grid.
The transition must also account for environmental safeguards, land-use pressures and the interests of communities whose livelihoods could be affected by new energy infrastructure.
The 2030 target presents an opportunity to diversify the electricity mix and reduce exposure to international fossil-fuel market volatility. However, turning that ambition into reality will require more than an increase in installed capacity. It will demand coordinated action on investment, project delivery, rooftop adoption, storage and grid modernization.
Shafiqul Alam, lead analyst for Bangladesh at IEEFA, told Dhaka Tribune that the 2030 renewable energy target was ambitious but achievable, provided the government accelerated implementation.
He said progress would depend largely on household uptake of rooftop solar incentives, available until February 2027, while industries were likely to move faster as rooftop solar could save them more than Tk7 per kilowatt-hour compared with grid electricity.
Timely completion of utility-scale projects and prioritizing grid modernization would also be crucial as the share of variable renewable energy increased.
He said the revised target of installing 10,450MW by 2030 would require an average addition of around 2,500MW annually.
Earlier, Imran Karim, former president of the Bangladesh Independent Power Producers' Association, estimated that Bangladesh would require $12 billion to $14 billion in investment to achieve its 20% renewable energy target by 2030.
Sharif Jamil, member secretary of DHORA and coordinator of Waterkeepers Bangladesh, called for a clear roadmap, effective measures and strong political commitment to achieve the government's target of generating 10,000MW of renewable electricity by 2030.
Farah Kabir, country director of ActionAid Bangladesh, said an equitable and inclusive energy transition was essential for sustainable development. She warned that Bangladesh's dependence on fossil fuels left its energy security vulnerable to international market volatility.
Professor Dr Eqramul Hoque, vice-chancellor of the Bangladesh University of Engineering and Technology (BUET), highlighted the economic pressure caused by rising international energy prices and called for universities and policymakers to work together to protect the environment and ensure affordable clean energy for future generations.
Power, Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Iqbal Hassan Mahmood said the government aimed to generate 10,000MW of renewable electricity by 2030 and was preparing a special Renewable Energy Law to facilitate decisions and implementation during 2026–2030.
“Due to excessive dependence on fossil fuels, global market volatility and the war in the Middle East have affected us. We have prepared a Special Renewable Energy Law to facilitate decisions and activities between 2026 and 2030 to ensure future energy security,” he said.
The minister said duties on solar technologies and equipment had been removed and that government incentives and affordable electricity-purchasing arrangements were being introduced to encourage rooftop solar installations.
He acknowledged that integrating electricity from nuclear, fossil-fuel and renewable sources remained challenging because the national power grid required further modernization.
The Power Grid Company of Bangladesh was working to modernize the grid, he said, expressing hope that Bangladesh would achieve the 10,000MW renewable energy target by 2030.

item.title: Naval police chief: Police to file case if Tahsif’s family does not
item.description:
The family of former flight lieutenant of Bangladesh Air Force KM Tahsif Sauri, has yet to file a case over his death, with police awaiting its decision.
However, if the family does not lodge a case, police will file one on their own initiative, Additional Inspector General of Police Md Rezaul Karim, chief of the Naval Police, has said.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Friday afternoon, he said police were waiting to see whether the family would take legal action. If not, police would file a case in accordance with the law.
He added that the Naval Police and the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) were jointly investigating the incident.
“PBI has taken one person into custody for questioning. Some information has been obtained and is now being verified,” he said.
KM Enayetul Karim, father of former Air Force officer Tahsif Sauri, has questioned the need for his family to file a case over his son's death, saying they do not want to get caught up in legal complications and repeated court visits.
Speaking to journalists on Friday, he said the family had yet to decide whether to file a case and would make a decision after discussing the matter among themselves.
“Why should we need to file a case? I believe the government will take responsibility and handle the matter with utmost sincerity. Filing a case in our country means a lot of hassle and repeated trips to court. Who wants to go through that when we have an excellent government?” he said.
He added that various government agencies were already working responsibly and actively on the matter.
Tahsif’s father has also questioned the account given by his friend Ahmed Shahriar Reza Dip about the circumstances surrounding his death.
Dip claimed that on the night of the incident, they fled after spotting two men who appeared to be police officers at the scene.
Dismissing the claim as absurd, Enayetul Karim questioned why a defence officer would run away from a police chase.
Speaking to journalists on Friday, he said: “Isn't that an absurd statement? I don't think he had ever been to that area. A defence officer would flee because of a police chase? Isn't that ridiculous? It simply doesn't make sense.”
A black motorcycle has emerged as a key piece of evidence in the investigation into the death of Tahsif Sauri.
Acting on information provided by Tahsif’s friend Dip, the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) recovered the motorcycle from the Mazar Basti area along the Turag River in Tongi.
According to the PBI, the motorcycle was found abandoned about 50 yards from the spot where Tahsif’s body was recovered.
PBI Dhaka Metro North Additional Deputy Inspector General Md Enayet Hossain Mannan disclosed the information to journalists on Friday.
PBI officials also visited the scene with Dip on the same day.

item.title: Saint Martin’s tourist travel postponed beyond November 1
item.description:
Tourist travel to Saint Martin’s Island will not resume on November 1 as scheduled due to delays in obtaining the necessary approvals for operating tourist vessels, with ship owners expecting services to begin on November 5 or 6.
Hossain Islam, general secretary of the Sea Cruise Operators Owners Association of Bangladesh, said vessels were yet to receive the required clearances from the relevant authorities.
According to the district administration and the Department of Environment, a decision on tourist travel to Saint Martin’s Island was taken at an inter-ministerial meeting held at the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change on October 12 this year.
A notification issued on October 25 retained the conditions imposed the previous year, requiring tourists to visit the island and return on the same day in November. Overnight stays were permitted in December and January.
The decision created confusion among tourists, hotel and restaurant owners, and ship operators.
The previous decision was subsequently revised through another notification issued on October 27. Signed by Sabrina Rahman, senior assistant secretary of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, the notification allowed tourists to visit and stay overnight on Saint Martin’s Island from November 1, 2026, to March 15, 2027.
It also set a daily limit of 3,500 tourists visiting the island.
Hossain Islam said operating vessels required clearance from the Ministry of Environment, approval from the Department of Shipping, a route permit from the Bangladesh Inland Water Transport Authority (BIWTA), and permission from the Cox’s Bazar deputy commissioner.
However, the approval process has yet to be completed. The software that the Bangladesh Tourism Board is supposed to launch to collect tourists’ information is also not ready.
As a result, vessels cannot operate from November 1. Preparations are underway to begin services on November 5 or 6, he said.
Foyezul Islam, acting chairman of Saint Martin’s Union Parishad, said several thousand residents of the island had been excited by the announcement that it would reopen to tourists from November 1.
More than 230 hotels, resorts, cottages and restaurants had been prepared to accommodate tourists staying overnight. However, ship services will not begin on November 1 as the vessels have yet to receive the necessary approvals.
Some expect services to begin between November 5 and 7, while others believe they may start on November 15, he said.
Cox’s Bazar Deputy Commissioner Md A Mannan said the administration was maintaining strict security measures for tourists visiting Saint Martin’s Island and Cox’s Bazar.
He said that although Saint Martin’s Island would reopen to tourists from November 1, vessels would be allowed to operate only after their fitness and safety were ensured.
A specific date for the resumption of ship services would be finalized at a meeting between the administration and ship owners at 11am on Saturday, he added.
The deputy commissioner said tourists would not be allowed to travel to Saint Martin’s Island by water from Teknaf, Shah Porir Dwip or Ukhiya. The only permitted departure point would be the BIWTA jetty in Cox’s Bazar.
Tourists would be allowed to visit the island only on government-approved vessels through online registration.
Referring to a tourist vessel fire last year, he said the relevant authorities were inspecting vessels to prevent a similar incident this year. Permission to operate would be granted after the inspections were completed.
Tourist vessels travelling to Saint Martin’s Island depart from the BIWTA jetty at Nuniachhara on the Bankkhali River in Cox’s Bazar town.
The island is approximately 120km from Nuniachhara, and the entire journey passes through the Bay of Bengal.

item.title: Tahsif Souri death: Friend says they were chased before he jumped into river
item.description:
Tahsif Souri, a former Bangladesh Air Force officer, was reportedly chased by a group of people shortly before he jumped into the Turag River, where his body was later recovered, according to a statement given to investigators by a friend.
Shahriar Dip, a friend of Tahsif, made the statement during questioning by the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI), which is conducting a parallel investigation alongside the Naval Police into Tahsif's death.
Earlier, on Thursday, Dip told journalists that he and Tahsif had gone to a garage together. He said they separated after having dinner in the House Building area of Uttara.
Dip also said that after returning home, he called Tahsif but found his mobile phone switched off. PBI officials are now trying to establish why his earlier account differs from the information he provided during questioning.
A PBI official holding the rank of superintendent of police said Dip told investigators: “We were talking there (at the scene). At that time, some people chased us. Tahsif bhai jumped into the river, and I ran away.”
The official said Dip's statement, along with other information obtained during questioning, was being verified.
On Friday, the PBI confirmed that Dip had been questioned. He was taken from his residence on Babar Road in Mohammadpur, Dhaka, to the PBI's Dhaka Metro North office on Thursday night.
The PBI official said investigators had conducted overnight operations at several locations with Dip to verify his account.
PBI chief Additional Inspector General of Police Mustafa Kamal said: “After taking Dip into custody, we have obtained several pieces of information.”
However, the PBI has not clarified whether Dip has been formally arrested.
Dip had spent around 6 hours with Tahsif before he went missing. Investigators are examining his account and trying to establish whether he was involved in Tahsif's disappearance and subsequent death.
The PBI said Dip's statements and the information he provided were being verified through on-site investigations and technological analysis.
On October 28, at around 4:30pm, Tongi River Police recovered Tahsif's floating body from the Rajabari Ghat area of the Turag River. His identity was confirmed through an iPhone and a wristwatch found near the body.
Tahsif's father, KM Enayetul Karim, suspects that his son was murdered. He said Tahsif had spent the entire day on October 27 shopping for his family before leaving home in the evening.
At 1:35am, Tahsif sent a text message to his mother saying: “Mum, I am coming.” His phone has remained switched off since then.
At around 5:15am, the family received news from police that his body had been recovered.
Tahsif's father said his son had never visited the Rajabari Ghat area before.
Meanwhile, no family members were found at Dip's residence on Babar Road. Security personnel responsible for the house said Dip was a student and that they knew little about his friendship with Tahsif.
They also said Dip returned home at around 2:30am on the night of the incident.

item.title: Father demands fair investigation into Tahsif Sauri's death
item.description:
The father of Tahsif Sauri, a dismissed flight lieutenant of the Bangladesh Air Force, has called for a fair investigation into his son's death to establish the actual cause.
“My son was a good citizen of this country and a member of the armed forces. I want a fair investigation into his death to uncover the truth,” KM Enayetul Karim told reporters on Friday afternoon.
He said no case had been filed over his son's death, adding that the family had yet to decide whether to pursue legal action.
Karim said filing a case was not the family's priority, urging the government to ensure a proper investigation under the relevant laws.
“As a family, we have not decided whether to file a case. We want the government to take action under its own legal framework rather than focus on whether we submit a written complaint at the police station,” he said.
Uttarkhan Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Habibur Rahman said he had contacted Tahsif's father and asked him to file a case, but he had yet to visit the police station.
Meanwhile, the Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) has taken Dip, identified as Tahsif's junior friend, into custody for questioning in connection with the death.
Dip reportedly spent around six hours with Tahsif before he went missing.

item.title: Bangladesh, UK discuss climate adaptation, renewable energy cooperation
item.description:
Bangladesh and the United Kingdom have discussed strengthening cooperation on climate adaptation and resilience, access to climate finance and the renewable energy transition to address shared climate challenges.
The issues featured at a meeting between State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam and the UK's Special Representative for Climate Rachel Kyte in London on Thursday, said a foreign ministry press release on friday.
The discussions covered opportunities for cooperation in carbon markets and investment in the green and blue economy, alongside efforts to strengthen climate resilience and accelerate the transition to renewable energy.
Shama highlighted Bangladesh's ongoing initiatives to enhance resilience, promote renewable energy and encourage community participation in climate action.
Both sides exchanged views on the disproportionate impacts of climate change on women and children and explored the potential for collaboration in climate-related technology and innovation.
They also stressed the importance of translating global climate commitments into practical action.
The meeting reviewed priorities for the upcoming COP31, with particular emphasis on climate finance, adaptation and enhanced cooperation to tackle shared climate challenges.
Bangladesh High Commissioner to the United Kingdom Ambassador Muhammad Abdul Muhith was also present.

item.title: Humaiun Kobir: No third country reference came up during PM's Japan visit
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir on Friday said no reference to any third country came up for discussion during Prime Minister’s just-concluded official visit to Japan, stressing that the visit focused exclusively on an economic partnership between the two countries.
"We made it very clear... no third country reference. We didn't go there to discuss the Bay of Bengal because the Bay of Bengal doesn't belong to us only," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, highlighting the achievements of the visit.
Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury, who is set to become the next Foreign Secretary and Additional Foreign Secretary (Public Diplomacy and Other Priority Matters), AKM Shahidul Karim were also present at the media briefing.
The state minister said Bangladesh is building a respectful bilateral economic partnership with Japan. "It's an investment-driven partnership."
In light of the rapidly changing global situation, increasing supply chain risks, rapid technological innovation and mounting social issues, Bangladesh and Japan agreed to upgrade BIG-B to “BIG-B for Shared Prosperity” as an initiative of “strategic cooperation” under the exclusive partnership between the two countries.
Responding to a question, Kobir said there was no scope for the government to go against the interests of the country and its people.
On the Rohingya issue, the state minister said it was an important national security issue and Bangladesh continued to raise it, as the solution to the problem lies in Myanmar.
The prime ministers of Bangladesh and Japan held a summit in Tokyo on Tuesday, followed by a joint press occasion and a luncheon.
The two leaders issued a “Japan-Bangladesh Joint Statement” after the summit meeting.
The Japanese prime minister congratulated Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on assuming office , describing him as a friend who shares the values of democracy.
She said that amid growing global instability, Japan strongly supports Bangladesh’s ability to make its own decisions and its resilience under the updated “Free and Open Indo-Pacific (FOIP)” and intends to further develop bilateral relations under the “Strategic Partnership”.
She also expressed her intention to work with Prime Minister Tarique Rahman towards peace and prosperity in the region.
In response, Prime Minister Rahman stated that Japan had followed the path of a peace-loving nation and was among the first countries to recognise Bangladesh’s independence.
He said Japan holds a special place in the hearts of the people of Bangladesh.
Rahman also said that Japan and Bangladesh had cultivated long-standing amicable relations and expressed his commitment to working together with Prime Minister Takaichi to take bilateral relations to new heights.
The two leaders concurred on upgrading the concept of the “Bay of Bengal Industrial Growth Belt (BIG-B)” into a new strategic cooperation initiative, “BIG-B for Shared Prosperity”, based on four pillars: (1) strengthening connectivity; (2) preparedness for natural disasters and geopolitical risks; (3) public-private partnerships for the co-creation of economic growth opportunities and rule-making; and (4) cooperation for peace and stability.
They also agreed to work together to make the Bay of Bengal region, with Bangladesh as its hub, a “region of shared prosperity”.
Prime Minister Takaichi said upcoming private investment by Japanese businesses in Bangladesh is projected to reach one trillion yen over the next five years, with an expected 200,000 jobs to be created, and expressed her intention to send a business mission to Bangladesh in the near future.
In response, Tarique Rahman said he welcomed and highly valued investment from Japanese businesses.
The two leaders agreed that their governments would work to ensure the early entry into force of the Japan-Bangladesh Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) and promote cooperation in areas such as trade and investment, agricultural, forestry and fishery products, the environment and climate change, as well as aviation.
Prime Minister Takaichi expressed her expectation that Prime Minister Rahman would provide leadership in creating an environment conducive to Japanese business activities and promoting public-private cooperation.
Prime Minister Rahman responded that the Government of Bangladesh would also work towards this goal in a transparent manner.
Regarding security, Prime Minister Takaichi announced that Japan had decided to provide a patrol vessel to enhance Bangladesh’s maritime security capabilities under Security-Contributing ODA.
The two leaders reaffirmed their commitment to continuing security and defence cooperation and working together to maintain peace and security in the region.
Prime Minister Rahman expressed his deep gratitude for the cooperation extended by the Government and people of Japan to Bangladesh to date and stated his intention to work towards “shared prosperity” for the two countries.
Reflecting on the cooperation between the two countries, which has expanded across a wide range of fields, including security, the economy and people-to-people exchanges, he expressed his intention to continue strengthening cooperation with Japan in various areas.

item.title: PBI: Tahsif, Deep went to Tongi slum together; only Deep returned
item.description:
The Police Bureau of Investigation (PBI) is questioning Ahmed Shahriar Reza Deep, a close friend of former flight lieutenant of Bangladesh Air Force K M Tahsif Souri, to uncover the circumstances surrounding his death.
According to information provided by Deep during questioning, the two travelled by motorcycle from Uttara to the Mazar slum area of Tongi on the night of the incident.
After spending some time there, Deep claimed he could not find Tahsif and eventually returned home alone on the motorcycle.
However, investigators have yet to establish why the two went to the area, what happened after they arrived or how they became separated. The PBI is now verifying Deep’s account to establish the sequence of events.
PBI Dhaka Metro North Inspector Sajedur Rahman shared the information with journalists on Friday afternoon at the Mazar slum area under Tongi West Police Station.
“Tahsif’s junior friend Deep is being questioned, and the process is still ongoing. He has provided various pieces of information.
According to him, they travelled by motorcycle from Uttara to the Mazar slum area of Tongi on the night of the incident and stayed there for some time. At one point, he could not find Tahsif and searched for him. Eventually, he returned home alone on the motorcycle,” Sajedur said.
The PBI official said Deep claimed to have reached home at around 2:30am. The following day, he learned that Tahsif’s body had been recovered near the river. The motorcycle was later recovered as part of the investigation.
“Both of them came here, and no one else was with them. Deep said they came from Uttara on a motorcycle to spend some time together. However, what happened after they arrived, where they went and why they became separated are still being investigated,” he added.
Asked whether Deep had been detained, Sajedur said he was not in custody but was being questioned to clarify the circumstances surrounding the incident.
“Initially, he was somewhat frightened, but later he provided various pieces of information. However, we are verifying different aspects of his statement,” he said.
Regarding the recovered motorcycle, the PBI inspector said it was found based on information provided by Deep.
Investigators would verify its ownership using the number plate and engine number.
He said it was too early to determine whether Tahsif's death was a murder, suicide or accident, adding that the actual cause would be established after receiving the autopsy report and other relevant medical information.
Tahsif Souri knew how to swim and had completed a specialised swimming course during his pilot training, for which he received a certificate.
His father, K M Enayetul Karim, has strongly rejected Deep's account to the PBI that Tahsif jumped into the river while being chased.
He believes attempts are being made to portray his son's death differently from what actually happened.
Asked whether he suspected a cover-up or conspiracy, Enayetul Karim said he believed efforts were being made to divert attention from the actual incident.
“Naturally, that is what it seems. Why would anyone chase him? An attempt is being made to take the incident in a different direction. I feel that efforts are underway to present the matter differently,” he said.
Earlier, on Tuesday evening, Tahsif left his home in Sector 18 of Uttara after Deep visited him. The two were later seen leaving on separate motorcycles.
According to the family, Tahsif left at Deep's invitation, and they have had no contact with him since.
On Wednesday, at around 4:30pm, River Police recovered Tahsif's body from the Turag River near Rajabari Ghat in Uttarkhan after receiving information through the national emergency helpline 999.
His relatives identified the body by the wristwatch and iPhone found in his pocket. It was subsequently sent to the morgue of Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital for an autopsy.

item.title: CHT minister for building drug and unemployment-free Bandarban
item.description:
Chittagong Hill Tracts (CHT) Affairs Minister Sa Ching Prue on Friday expressed his determination to ensure balanced development of the CHT, create employment and build an unemployment-free Bandarban.
At the same time, he called upon leaders and activists of Jubo Dal to remain united to build a drug-free Bangladesh and a drug-free Bandarban hill district.
The minister said this while addressing a youth rally as the chief guest at the Press Club premises, held after a rally organised by the Bandarban District Jubo Dal to mark the 48th founding anniversary of Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Jubo Dal, according to a PID release.
He said the harmful impact of drugs is increasing day by day everywhere in the country and drugs have now become a national problem. Although Cox's Bazar has been identified as the main route of drugs, its serious impact is being seen in the CHT, including Naikhongchhari, Alikadam and Thanchi, he said.
Outlining the future development plans for Bandarban, the minister said balanced development of the CHT must be ensured without being driven by emotion, by keeping the bonds of amity and harmony strong.
He said extensive employment opportunities will be created in Bandarban by taking everyone along, irrespective of party and opinion.
"By adopting specific and coordinated plans, we want to build a completely unemployment-free Bandarban," he said.
Bandarban District Jubo Dal President Zahir Uddin Masum presided over the rally, while the district Jubo Dal General Secretary Md Ariful Islam Chowdhury moderated it.
A large number of leaders and activists of the Bandarban unit of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) and its various associate organisations were present at the programme.

item.title: Tuku: Govt working to ensure healthcare services for disadvantaged people
item.description:
State Minister for Fisheries and Livestock Sultan Salahuddin Tuku has said the government is prioritising efforts to ensure healthcare assistance and development programmes reach disadvantaged people at the grassroots level.
He said Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has placed particular emphasis on supporting underprivileged people, especially those suffering from cancer, kidney disease and other critical illnesses, by providing financial assistance for their treatment.
Tuku made the remarks on Friday afternoon while distributing cheques among poor patients suffering from cancer, kidney disease and other complex illnesses at the Tangail Sadar Upazila Parishad building.
He said anyone suffering from a serious illness who had not yet received medical assistance could apply for support, pledging to take all possible steps to help them. “The programme will continue. We are committed to the people and will continue working for their welfare,” he said.
The state minister added that the scope of government assistance had expanded across various sectors since the BNP assumed office. Initiatives include family cards, farmer cards and allowances for imams and muezzins, alongside development activities across the country.
He said the government was taking all possible measures to ensure that public services and assistance reached people at the grassroots level.
At the programme, six patients each received Tk100,000, bringing the total amount distributed to Tk600,000.
Tangail Sadar Upazila Nirbahi Officer Shaheen Mia chaired the event. Among those present were former Tangail district BNP general secretary Mahmudul Haque Sanu, Tangail Sadar Thana BNP President Azgar Ali, former district BNP organising secretaries Ashraf Paheli and Shafiqul Rahman Shafik, and Tangail district Jubo Dal Convener Khandaker Rashedul Alam Rashed.
Union parishad chairmen, leaders and activists of the BNP and its affiliated organisations, and local dignitaries also attended.
After the cheque distribution, Tuku inaugurated a visitors' room at his office as part of efforts to improve public access to services and make government activities more accessible.

item.title: Off-spinners hold sway as Chase leaves Bangladesh reeling
item.description:
West Indies captain Roston Chase led the spin assault, dismantling Bangladesh's top order to leave the hosts reeling at 79-6 on the third day of the first Test in Mirpur on Friday.
Bangladesh held a 106-run lead at stumps, with concussion substitute Jaker Ali and Nayeem Hasan -- both on 18 -- at the crease when bad light stopped play early.
Earlier, off-spinner Nayeem took four wickets to bowl West Indies out for 245, conceding a lead of 27 runs in response to Bangladesh's first-innings total of 272.
"We are in a very good position," West Indies batting coach Floyd Reifer said after the day's play.
"We bowled in disciplined areas, stuck to the team plans and everyone really hustled out there in the heat."
Reifer added: "If we're going to chase 125 runs, I think that's really possible for us on a pitch like that. But obviously, you have to get early wickets."
West Indies resumed the day on 134-4 and continued to frustrate Bangladesh through a fifth-wicket partnership between Tagenarine Chanderpaul, who top-scored with 56, and Justin Greaves.
The pair added 65 runs before Shoriful Islam broke the stand, with Chanderpaul edging to second slip where captain Najmul Hossain Shanto took a sharp catch.
Bangladesh had to wait for another breakthrough as Greaves kept up the defiance with skipper Chase, who made an unbeaten 43 after being dropped on 27, for company.
Off-spinner Nayeem broke through by trapping Greaves lbw for 46 shortly before lunch, leaving West Indies at 213-6.
Chase came out attacking, while Joshua Bishop contributed 15 before being stumped off Mehidy Hasan Miraz.
Bishop had earlier been dropped on 11 by Mominul Haque at short leg, with the Bangladesh batter suffering concussion while attempting the catch. He was replaced by Jaker.
Nayeem, who took 4-33, then cleaned up the tail, removing Shamar Joseph and Jomel Warrican in the 81st over before dismissing Jayden Seales in the next.
West Indies fast bowler Joseph struck in the second over to send back opener Tanzid Hasan for a duck.
Shadman Islam, who scored 105 in the first innings, and Shanto briefly steadied things before Chase took control and bowled the opener for 13.
Chase had Towhid Hridoy out for a duck two balls later and trapped skipper Najmul Hossain Shanto lbw for 10 in his next over to leave Bangladesh tottering at 33-4 before rain interrupted play for around 30 minutes.
West Indies continued their assault after the break as Warrican trapped Litton Das lbw for four before bowling Mehidy Hasan Miraz to reduce Bangladesh to 53-6.
"We will try to give the team as many runs as possible," said Nayeem. "A total of 200 would be very good. We will try to score even more."

item.title: Thousands of students, workers protest in Italy under heavy security
item.description:
Thousands of students and workers took to the streets across Italy on Friday, calling for more school funding and relief from the soaring cost of living, amid a high police presence to avert possible clashes.
Friday’s Italy-wide protest comes after weeks of demonstrations, led by students who have set up tent camps and occupied schools to make their demands heard, fueled by similar movements in nearby France and Spain.
A general strike called by Italy’s USB trade union attracted thousands of workers to Friday’s protests, including truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers who have rallied in recent weeks over the spike in fuel prices and to oppose rising defense spending.
Marches were held in dozens of cities up and down the country, including in Bologna, Genoa, Naples, and Turin -- where a few minor skirmishes between protesters and riot police occurred at the start of the protest.
In Rome, university student Beatrice Chilelli told AFP students were “at a breaking point.”
“They can’t afford to pay exorbitant tuition fees, and rent... which weighs heavily on their parents’ shoulders,” said the 21-year-old, citing student housing in Rome that could reach 1,200 euros per month for a single room.
Thousands of people left Rome’s central Termini train station, accompanied by two tractors and a taxi, making their way past the Colosseum as they waved flags, unfurled banners and shouted into megaphones.
An AFP photographer witnessed a heavy police presence outside the Economy Ministry, which the procession passed by.
“We need more houses, not bombs!” sang one group in the crowd, as a troupe of protesters gave a brief performance imitating terrified civilians in a Gaza bombing raid.
The Milan protest also began at the central train station, but then headed outside the city -- far from the center where young vandals had looted stores, destroyed property and clashed with police two weeks ago after another sanctioned cost-of-living demonstration.
“Let’s reclaim our future” read one banner unfurled by students in Milan.
Police in riot gear blocked off streets, but no major clashes had been reported as of midday.
Besides students, the demonstrators at Friday’s protest included teachers, workers and retired people, with one man in Rome bearing a sign that read “Pensioners - Pissed Off and Furious.”
Many pro-Palestine flags were seen in the crowds in major cities.
Ahead of the demonstration, a spokesperson for the OSA student movement, 18-year-old Laura Teresi, told AFP she expected a “massive” mobilization that would empty out schools.
“We will take to the streets to denounce the rearmament policies of (Prime Minister Giorgia) Meloni’s government and the rising cost of living, which is weighing ever more heavily on families, workers and students,” she added.
The students will also protest against the “endless budget cuts to teaching”, Teresi said.
Following the October 17-18 weekend of clashes between youth and police in Milan, Meloni’s hard-right government toughened laws on public gatherings while easing rules on detaining minors.
The government also last week agreed on a $195 million aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.
Measures in favor of young people and families are also planned in the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties, such as an annual bonus of 2,500 euros for workers under 30.
“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general... who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Meloni said at a press conference on Wednesday, stressing that these measures were “not for those who smash windows.”

item.title: Iran Guards say two tankers halted after ‘incidents’ in Hormuz
item.description:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards on Friday said two oil tankers had been halted after encountering unspecified “incidents” while attempting to transit what Tehran considers an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz.
“Two offending oil tankers, one in the eastern part and the other in the western part of the Strait of Hormuz, which were attempting to pass through the unauthorized route, encountered incidents and were brought to a halt in the waters south of the strait,” the IRGC said in a statement.
The tankers had “switched off all their navigation and positioning systems and, with the support of the terrorist US military, were attempting to exit through the unauthorized route,” the statement added.
The Guards did not specify the nature of the incidents, which came a day after Iran’s armed forces said at least four tankers had stopped in the area after hitting mines.
They said Friday’s incidents occurred after the vessels received several radio warnings but disregarded them.
Iranian forces have demanded that vessels use a designated route through the strait and coordinate their passage with the country’s armed forces, labelling a southern corridor closer to Oman’s shores as unauthorized.
Iran has restricted maritime traffic through the strategic waterway since the Middle East war began on February 28 with US-Israeli strikes on Iran that killed former supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The United States has in turn imposed a blockade on Iranian ports, further restricting Tehran’s ability to export oil and conduct trade.

item.title: Venezuela: Opposition leader Machado says US backs 2027 election
item.description:
Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado said on Thursday that the country was moving towards a US-prescribed presidential election in 2027, in her first public remarks since returning from 10 months in exile.
Calling the transition to democracy “irreversible,” Machado said, “US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a sequence of steps for moving toward a democratic transition that includes ​presidential elections in 2027.”
“The date of the election is the date of liberation,” Machado said in Caracas after returning home following 10 months in exile.
Machado also reiterated that her priorities included dismantling the country’s repressive system and securing the release of the thousands of political prisoners. She denied having had any contact with interim President Delcy Rodriguez.
Shortly before Machado’s public statements, Rodriguez announced that there “will be elections” in Venezuela, without specifying a date.
Machado, who famously “presented” US President Donald Trump with her Nobel Peace Prize, thanked Trump for his actions on January 3, leading to “the floodgate to freedom” being opened in Venezuela.
The opposition leader was referring to the US capture of former President Nicolas Maduro, currently facing US drug trafficking and torture charges, which he denies.
Machado, however, criticized a major oil deal Washington and Caracas agreed to earlier this year, under which Venezuela is expected to supply 20% of its oil reserves to the United States.
“This agreement does not reflect the levels of transparency that Venezuelan society wants,” she said.
At the same time, she skirted questions that highlighted Trump’s comments in January that she did not have sufficient support to immediately lead Venezuela, as well as his suggestion this week that the country could become the 51st US state.
Machado, who was barred from contesting the 2024 presidential election, backed opposition candidate Edmundo Gonzalez. His supporters said he had won by a wide margin, even though electoral authorities declared Maduro the winner.
Machado’s recent return after nearly a year in exile complicates things for Washington which has said Machado has every right to be in Venezuela, but also praised acting President Rodriguez.

item.title: Journalists say press freedom in India under attack from government
item.description:
Journalist Shoaib Daniyal had barely stepped out his door when he saw the police checkpoint at the end of his driveway. It hadn’t been there the previous day.
So, the 40-year-old struck up a conversation with the officer about the protest he was heading to for work.
“He became suspicious, he became angry [and] said, ‘I’m going to detain you.’”
Indian laws allow police to detain people without a warrant in certain circumstances if they reasonably suspect someone has committed, or will commit, a crime.
But Daniyal said no explanation was provided before he was hauled onto a bus.
The Committee to Protect Journalists reported 43 reporters had been detained across the country over two days in October, most of them in the capital.
While India sits at 157 out of 180 countries in press freedom rankings, down from 140 in 2019, according to the Reporters Without Borders World Press Freedom Index, journalists who spoke to the ABC said watching police push, pull and carry reporters onto buses was something they never anticipated seeing in Delhi.
“In the national capital, where you have such a concentration of journalists, you would not have a government that would feel confident enough to do this because of the outrage it would evoke,” said Manisha Pande, editor-in-chief of digital news company Newslaundry.
The detentions come as Prime Minister Narendra Modi faces one of the biggest challenges to his leadership since taking power in 2014.
This month, demonstrators held rallies across the country calling for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, alleging a national revision of voter rolls was being used to favor the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
It was the second wave of major protests in India this year, after the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party successfully ousted India’s education minister in July over ongoing exam paper leaks.
But the pressure on journalists extends well beyond the recent demonstrations.
Some journalists say the government has steadily tightened its grip on the media since BJP came to power in 2014.
“The media in India has never been entirely free, it’s always come under extraordinary strain from government,” said Sreenivasan Jain, an author and journalist who has reported in India for more than 30 years.
“But what I’ve witnessed in the past decade or so is a complete collapse. Entire swaths of, particularly TV media, have been brought to heel, have turned into propagandists for the government.”
Pande compared India’s prime-time broadcast news landscape to having “multiple Fox News” channels.
“Channel after channel that will have the same talking points praising the government, rarely ever questioning it, hammering at the opposition, going at people who protest, calling dissenters enemies of the country,” she said.
She said anchors who repeated government talking points were often rewarded with coveted interviews with ministers or the prime minister.
The dominance of pro-government television news has given rise to the term “Godi media”, which means lapdog media.
Corporate ownership and government advertising have added another layer of pressure.
Many television networks depend on government advertising revenue and are owned by corporations with business interests tied to government contracts.
Jain spent 30 years as a reporter and anchor at NDTV, once widely considered one of the last traditional television networks openly critical of Mr Modi.
He left in 2022 after the network was taken over by the Adani Group, which is owned by billionaire Gautam Adani, who has a close relationship with Narendra Modi.
“In a matter of weeks, it was pretty clear what kind of direction they wanted to take the network,” he said.
Among the red flags, he said, was pressure to broadcast an interview Mr Adani had given to a rival network, despite objections from journalists.
“I didn’t want, for a second, to be around [those] endorsing those sorts of editorial practices,” he said.
Pande said young Indians were increasingly rejecting the television news their parents had consumed for years.
“You have a generation that is … revolted by the idea of what television news has [reported] over the last 12 years, which is not talking about issues that concern them [like] education, jobs [and] infrastructure,” she said.
That disillusionment has created an opening for independent digital news platforms and creators publishing on social media platforms like YouTube, Instagram and X.
Among them is 35-year-old political satirist Ramit Verma, who was recently detained while covering the protests in Delhi.
He wants more Indians to document events to help hold those in power accountable.
“Everyone is [a] journalist, especially in India right now, where the mainstream media is so sold out and so dangerous,” Verma said.
Jain believed the recent detentions of journalists were the response of “a wounded regime”.
“They wanted to stamp out the protests using extraordinary force, and I think silencing or trying to intimidate the media in these new ways is part of that response,” he said.
The ABC has contacted Delhi police and the Modi government for comment.
According to the Indian Express newspaper, the Modi government has also ordered close to 195,000 take down orders on posts shared on Instagram, Facebook and YouTube between March and July.
Verma said he had lost count of how many of his own posts had been censored.
“It happens so much that I don’t even remember the last post that got taken down,” he said.
“But it’s become the norm in India right now. It’s become a norm for your post to get taken down at any point. Without any explanation, especially from Meta.”
The restrictions have also extended to foreign media organizations trying to report on the government.
Major international broadcasters, including the BBC and Al Jazeera, have faced requirements to establish Indian entities and employ local staff to continue operating in the country.
Foreign journalists also face tighter geographical restrictions, with government permits required to enter certain regions, including Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh.
The government is also trying to pass new privacy laws which would force journalists to ask permission before naming anyone in a story.
They have been labelled pre-censorship laws by the Digital News Publishers Association, which is representing a group of 21 news publishers in India’s Supreme Court arguing the law must exempt journalists to protect press freedom.
For Daniyal, the detention of reporters on the streets of the national capital is the latest sign of how much the environment has changed.
“For the last 12 years, the fear that journalists feel has really shot up,” he said.
“This idea that journalists are doing a critical job for democracy, the foundation of that has [been] shaken.”

item.title: Fire pollution killed 3,560 people in Indonesia in September
item.description:
Pollution from smoke emitted by months of wildfires across Indonesia caused an estimated 3,560 deaths in the vast Southeast Asian archipelago in September, according to a new study.
The same month, about 57.8 million people in Indonesia were inhaling unhealthy to hazardous air, said the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (Crea), a Helsinki-based think tank.
“Worsening air quality due to forest and land fires in Indonesia pushed the estimated death toll to 3,560 cases in September 2026, a twofold increase from the August estimate,” said a Crea statement on Thursday.
The Crea study estimated the number of deaths brought about by PM2.5 pollution in the short-term, meaning a matter of days.
PM2.5 particles are small enough to penetrate the lungs or bloodstream and the World Health Organization has linked exposure to a higher risk for illness and premature death.
Most estimated deaths occurred on Indonesia’s part of Borneo island as well as on Java and Sumatra islands and in the country’s east, said the report.
The researchers also looked at non-fire pollution from urban power generation, industry, and transportation, and found it had caused a further 1,750 deaths in September for a total of 5,310 in the country of about 290 million people.
“In September alone, exposure levels breached the WHO annual PM2.5 threshold... by over seven times nationally, 10 times in Sumatra, and an alarming 24 times in Kalimantan” in Borneo, said the report.
More than 330,000 cases of acute respiratory infection have been recorded countrywide.
Gripped by drought worsened by the El Nino weather phenomenon, Indonesia has for months battled wildfires that deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas says have consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September.
The government has not confirmed or rejected the number.
The resulting haze has sent pollution levels soaring as far afield as Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and East Timor, clouding Indonesia’s ties with its neighbors.
Experts say the wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices, often by timber, palm oil or mining companies.
For the island of Java, the most populated and home to the capital Jakarta, the CREA report said between 73 and 80 percent of air pollution deaths -- a total of 1,530 in September -- were attributed to non-fire sources such as industry, vehicle emissions, and waste burning.
“These figures underscore the stark reality that non-fire air pollution sources are as dangerous as smoke from burning forests and peatlands,” it said.
In the report, the CEO of Landscape Indonesia consultancy, Agus Sari, pointed to the government’s “weak preparedness” for what he described as a “predictable and avoidable” disaster.
Agus pointed to budget cuts hampering the efforts of the BNPB national disaster management agency.
“Indonesia should be able to prepare for what is going to happen. The fact that we are not prepared at all is purely a matter of lacking the will,” said Agus.
The CREA report argued the government needs to shift from wildfire response to the restoration of peatlands left fire prone by extensive draining.
“This step must be accompanied by firm law enforcement against illegal land clearing through burning, as well as strengthened legal accountability for concession holders to prevent damage,” it said.
For regions battling non-fire pollution, such as Java, it said the government must enforce stricter emissions standards.
The government on Wednesday defended its approach to the fires, saying in a statement more than 72,000 people had been deployed in cloud-seeding and firefighting operations, more than 2,100 doctors and health workers activated in hard-hit areas, and 5.3 million masks distributed.

item.title: How Trump could interfere in US midterm elections
item.description:
State officials who run US elections are bracing for further intervention by President Donald Trump’s administration in next week’s midterms -- fearing federal authorities could disrupt voting, challenge ballot counts or try to block unfavorable results.
Trump, whose Republicans face an uphill battle to keep control of Congress, has repeatedly questioned the integrity of US elections and urged his party to “nationalize” voting in at least 15 places.
The White House says it is protecting election security, and many of the feared scenarios remain hypothetical. The US Constitution gives the president no direct role in running elections, and federal courts have so far rebuffed the administration’s main legal challenges.
Here are the key potential flashpoints:
Voter eligibility: The Justice Department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to obtain their voter registration lists, saying it needs them to find non-citizens. It has lost more than two dozen of those cases.
It has also demanded that ballots be set aside from about 20,000 people in California and more than 400 in Washington state whom it suspects are non-citizens.
A federal judge rejected the California request on Wednesday, saying it would wreak havoc on an election already underway. Washington state has also refused the demand.
Studies have repeatedly found non-citizen voting to be exceptionally rare.
Pressure on officials: The Justice Department has warned election officials in every state that they could face prosecution if they knowingly allow non-citizens to vote.
And Trump on Monday offered $1 million for information leading to a voter fraud conviction, without giving details.
Federal monitors: The Justice Department plans to send around 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states -- its largest deployment ever.
Monitoring is a decades-old practice, but Democrats and voting rights groups fear monitors could intimidate voters. The department says they will be unarmed, barred from interfering with voting and drawn from neither the FBI nor Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).
Immigration agents and troops: Advocates fear ICE operations near polling stations could deter voters in immigrant communities.
The administration says it is not planning operations targeting polling places, although Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said ICE agents could serve warrants there.
Trump has declined to rule out declaring a national emergency or invoking the Insurrection Act, which allows the president to deploy troops at home.
A Civil War-era law bars troops and armed federal agents from polling places, and legal experts say an emergency declaration would not give the president power over elections.
Seizing election materials: Federal agents could seek warrants or subpoenas for ballots, voting machines or records -- potentially disrupting the count.
In January, the FBI seized ballots and other 2020 election records in Fulton County, Georgia, a focus of Trump’s false claims that he won that year.
Election officials warn that similar action during an active count could undermine safeguards tracking how ballots are handled.
Challenging the count: Trump could allege fraud involving mail-in ballots, voting machines or votes counted after election night, fueling demands for recounts or attempts to halt counting.
But the US Supreme Court ruled in June that states may count mail ballots postmarked by election day that arrive afterward, and courts can intervene against unlawful disruption.
Blocking certification: The Justice Department has sued Alaska to delay certification of its Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan narrowly loses to Democrat Mary Peltola, citing a second candidate named Dan Sullivan who it says is trying to confuse voters, which he denies.
Trump said he ordered the lawsuit.
Experts say federal law does not allow the department to block certification, which courts can compel officials to carry out.
Challenging Democratic victories: Trump could pressure state officials to dispute results, as he did after losing the 2020 election.
Experts warn unresolved disputes could also delay the seating of newly elected lawmakers in January.
But courts have repeatedly upheld states’ authority over elections, and Democrats and voting rights groups have assembled legal teams to fight any interference.
